objectives: Map the four chambers, four valves, and the right and left coronary circulation.
Trace an electrical impulse through the SA node, AV node, His-Purkinje system.
Describe the five phases of the cardiac action potential and the ionic basis of pacemaker automaticity.

slides.title: Chambers, valves, and the great vessels
slides.body:
The heart is two pumps in series, each with an atrium and a ventricle, separated by a connective-tissue **cardiac skeleton** that electrically insulates the atria from the ventricles.

**The right heart** receives deoxygenated systemic blood. The **superior** and **inferior vena cavae** empty into the **right atrium**; blood crosses the **tricuspid valve** into the **right ventricle**, then is ejected through the **pulmonary valve** into the **pulmonary artery** toward the lungs. **The left heart** receives oxygenated blood: the four **pulmonary veins** drain into the **left atrium**; blood crosses the **mitral valve** (the bicuspid valve) into the **left ventricle**, the thickest chamber, and is ejected through the **aortic valve** into the **aorta**.

Valves fall into two classes. The two **atrioventricular (AV) valves** — tricuspid and mitral — are tethered by **chordae tendineae** to **papillary muscles** that prevent prolapse during systole. The two **semilunar valves** — pulmonary and aortic — have three cusps each and snap shut under back-pressure at the start of diastole. The closing of AV valves produces the first heart sound **S1** ('lub'); the closing of semilunar valves produces the second heart sound **S2** ('dub').

The heart muscle feeds itself through the **coronary arteries**, the first branches off the aorta just above the aortic valve, at the sinuses of **Valsalva**. The **right coronary artery (RCA)** supplies the right ventricle, the inferior wall, and in most people the **SA node** and **AV node**; it gives off the **posterior descending artery** in the ~85% of people with 'right-dominant' circulation. The **left main coronary artery** divides into the **left anterior descending (LAD)** — feeding the anterior wall, the apex, and most of the interventricular septum — and the **left circumflex (LCx)**, feeding the lateral and posterior left ventricle. Coronary perfusion is unusual in occurring chiefly during **diastole**, because during systole the contracting myocardium squeezes its own vessels shut. This is why a fast heart rate, which shortens diastole, can starve the subendocardium of blood — the mechanistic root of demand **ischemia**. The venous return drains via the **coronary sinus** into the right atrium. This anatomy explains the territorial logic of heart attacks: an LAD occlusion threatens the large anterior wall (the classic 'widow-maker'), whereas an RCA occlusion often disturbs rate and rhythm by depriving the nodes.

slides.title: The conduction system: SA node to Purkinje fibers
slides.body:
An ordinary contraction is choreographed by a dedicated network of specialized myocytes that generate and distribute electrical impulses. Anatomists **Wilhelm His Jr.** (who described the AV bundle in 1893), **Sunao Tawara** (who clarified the AV node and conducting bundle in 1906), **Arthur Keith** and **Martin Flack** (who identified the **sinoatrial node** in 1907), and **Jan Evangelista Purkinje** (who described the terminal fibers in 1839) mapped this system.

The impulse follows a fixed path:

- **1. Sinoatrial (SA) node.** Sitting in the right atrium near the entry of the superior vena cava, the SA node is the heart's natural **pacemaker**, firing spontaneously about 60-100 times per minute. It sets the **sinus rhythm**.
- **2. Atrial spread and internodal tracts.** The impulse spreads across both atria, causing atrial contraction (the ECG **P wave**), and converges on the AV node, partly guided by **Bachmann's bundle** to the left atrium.
- **3. Atrioventricular (AV) node.** Located at the floor of the right atrium near the tricuspid valve, the AV node is the sole normal electrical bridge across the insulating cardiac skeleton. It deliberately **delays** conduction by about 0.1 s (the **PR interval** on the ECG), giving the atria time to finish emptying into the ventricles before they contract. It also protects the ventricles by filtering out excessively fast atrial rates.
- **4. Bundle of His.** The signal passes into the **bundle of His**, which dives into the interventricular septum.
- **5. Bundle branches.** It splits into the **right bundle branch** and the **left bundle branch** (the left further divides into anterior and posterior fascicles), racing down either side of the septum.
- **6. Purkinje fibers.** These terminal fibers fan out across the ventricular endocardium, depolarizing the ventricular muscle from apex to base almost simultaneously — the ECG **QRS complex** — so the ventricles contract as a coordinated unit, wringing blood upward toward the outflow valves.

Conduction velocities differ enormously by tissue: the **AV node** is slow (~0.05 m/s, the bottleneck), atrial and ventricular muscle conduct at ~0.5-1 m/s, and the **Purkinje system** is the fastest at ~2-4 m/s. This hierarchy guarantees orderly, sequential contraction. A failure anywhere — a blocked bundle branch, a diseased AV node — distorts the QRS or interrupts the relay, the basis of **bundle-branch blocks** and **heart block**.

slides.title: The cardiac action potential and pacemaker automaticity
slides.body:
Cardiac myocytes have a strikingly different action potential from neurons: it lasts roughly **200-300 ms** (versus ~1 ms in nerve), because a long **plateau** keeps the cell depolarized. This plateau forces a long **refractory period** that prevents tetanic (sustained) contraction and protects against premature re-excitation. The ventricular action potential has five phases, defined by the dominant ion currents.

- **Phase 0 (upstroke).** A fast inward **sodium current** ($I_{Na}$) through voltage-gated Na channels rockets the membrane from about $-90$ mV up past 0 mV. This is what spreads cell-to-cell through **gap junctions** (connexin-43).
- **Phase 1 (early repolarization).** Na channels inactivate and a brief outward potassium current ($I_{to}$, the transient outward current) nicks the potential downward.
- **Phase 2 (plateau).** The signature of cardiac muscle: inward **L-type calcium current** ($I_{Ca,L}$, through dihydropyridine-sensitive Cav1.2 channels) balances outward potassium currents, holding voltage near 0 mV. This Ca influx triggers **calcium-induced calcium release** from the sarcoplasmic reticulum via **ryanodine receptors**, the trigger for contraction (excitation-contraction coupling, elucidated by **Setsuro Ebashi** and others).
- **Phase 3 (repolarization).** Ca channels close while delayed-rectifier potassium currents ($I_{Kr}$ and $I_{Ks}$) dominate, returning the cell toward rest. The **hERG** channel carrying $I_{Kr}$ is the one blocked by many drugs to cause acquired long-QT.
- **Phase 4 (resting potential).** In working myocardium the membrane sits stably at about $-90$ mV, set by the inward-rectifier potassium current $I_{K1}$.

**Pacemaker cells** in the SA and AV nodes behave differently: they have **no stable phase 4**. Instead they show **automaticity** — a slow spontaneous depolarization called the **diastolic depolarization** or pacemaker potential, driven largely by the **funny current** ($I_f$), a mixed Na/K inward current through **HCN channels** (hyperpolarization-activated, cyclic-nucleotide-gated) discovered and named by **Dario DiFrancesco**. As $I_f$ slowly drifts the membrane upward, it reaches threshold and fires, then resets — a self-restarting oscillator. Their upstroke (phase 0) is carried by **calcium**, not sodium, so it is slower. The SA node has the fastest intrinsic rate and so normally **overdrives** all slower potential pacemakers; if it fails, the AV junction (~40-60 bpm) or the ventricles (~20-40 bpm) take over as escape pacemakers. Autonomic tone tunes the rate: **acetylcholine** from the **vagus nerve** slows $I_f$ and opens $I_{K,ACh}$ to slow the heart, while **norepinephrine** steepens the pacemaker slope to speed it. The drug **ivabradine** selectively blocks $I_f$ to slow the SA node without affecting contractility — a direct clinical exploitation of the funny current.

question.question: Why does the atrioventricular (AV) node deliberately delay the electrical impulse by about 0.1 second?
options: To allow the SA node time to recharge before the next beat
To allow the atria to finish emptying into the ventricles before ventricular contraction
To increase the conduction velocity into the Purkinje fibers
To prevent the coronary arteries from being compressed
question.explanation: The AV nodal delay (seen as the PR interval) gives the atria time to complete ventricular filling — the 'atrial kick' — before the ventricles contract. It also filters very fast atrial rates to protect the ventricles. It does not recharge the SA node, and the delay slows, not speeds, conduction at the node itself.

hints: Think about the timing of atrial versus ventricular contraction.
The delay optimizes ventricular filling before ejection begins.
slides.workedSolution: The AV node is the only normal electrical bridge across the insulating cardiac skeleton, and its ~0.1 s delay (the PR interval) ensures the atria empty fully into the ventricles before ventricular systole, maximizing end-diastolic volume and thus stroke volume by Frank-Starling.

question.question: During which phase of the ventricular action potential does the inward L-type calcium current balance outward potassium currents to produce the characteristic plateau?
question.explanation: Phase 2 is the plateau, sustained by inward L-type Ca current (I_Ca,L) opposing outward K currents. This calcium influx triggers calcium-induced calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Phase 0 is the Na upstroke, phase 1 is early repolarization (I_to), and phase 4 is the resting potential set by I_K1.

hints: The plateau is unique to cardiac muscle and depends on calcium.
It is the phase between the rapid upstroke and final repolarization.
slides.workedSolution: Phase 2, the plateau, is driven by L-type Ca current. The Ca that enters triggers ryanodine-receptor calcium release, coupling excitation to contraction. The long plateau is what gives cardiac muscle its protective refractory period.

question.question: If the SA node fails completely and a ventricular escape pacemaker takes over firing at one impulse every 1.5 seconds, what is the resulting heart rate in beats per minute?
question.hint: Heart rate in bpm equals 60 seconds divided by the interval between beats in seconds.

question.question: An inferior heart attack with a slow pulse
question.prompt: A 64-year-old presents with chest pain and an inferior-wall myocardial infarction. His ECG shows the inferior leads affected, and his heart rate is only 38 bpm with evidence of AV block. Knowing that in most people one particular coronary artery supplies both the inferior wall AND the SA and AV nodes, identify the likely culprit vessel and explain mechanistically why an occlusion there produces both the inferior infarct pattern and the bradyarrhythmia. What backup pacemaker is most likely generating his 38 bpm rhythm, and why is its rate so much slower than normal sinus rhythm?

question.question: The 'funny current' (I_f) responsible for the spontaneous diastolic depolarization of pacemaker cells flows through which channel, and which drug selectively blocks it?
options: L-type calcium channels, blocked by amlodipine
hERG potassium channels, blocked by sotalol
Fast sodium channels, blocked by lidocaine
question.explanation: The funny current I_f, characterized by Dario DiFrancesco, flows through HCN channels (hyperpolarization-activated, cyclic-nucleotide-gated) and drives the pacemaker potential. Ivabradine selectively blocks I_f to slow the SA node without reducing contractility. hERG carries I_Kr (phase 3), and fast Na channels carry phase 0 in working myocardium.

hints: The current is named for its unusual activation on hyperpolarization.
The blocking drug slows heart rate without negative inotropy.
slides.workedSolution: I_f flows through HCN channels; ivabradine is the selective blocker used clinically to lower heart rate in angina and heart failure while sparing contractility — a clean pharmacological readout of the pacemaker mechanism DiFrancesco described.
